name: Mazu (Goddess of the Sea)
domain: Protector of the seas, maritime safety, universal blessings
description: Every year in the third lunar month, a human dragon stretches for miles down the highways of central Taiwan: hundreds of thousands of pilgrims walking behind a single palanquin, nine days and eight nights, more than 300 kilometers on foot. Inside that palanquin rides Mazu — formally the Heavenly Holy Mother, also called Tianhou or the Empress of Heaven, and affectionately known as 'Mazu Po,' Grandmother Mazu. She was born Lin Mo-niang, the daughter of a fishing family on Meizhou Island in Fujian during the Northern Song dynasty. In life she saved countless people and could read the coming storms; after her death, the coastal communities enshrined her as the goddess who guards those at sea. Ming and Qing settlers staked their lives on that faith as they crossed the treacherous Taiwan Strait, and built temples in gratitude once they landed safely — which is why Taiwan today holds more than a thousand Mazu temples, one in nearly every coastal town. By now her care reaches far beyond the water: fishermen pray for safe returns, merchants for good business, students for passing grades, and some even come to ask for a spouse or a child. People call her the shared mother of Taiwan — and once you've seen the frenzy of 'March Mazu madness,' the title feels earned.
story:
The most wrenching moment in Mazu's legend happens at a loom. Lin Mo-niang was weaving one day when her eyes suddenly closed and she slumped forward, her face gone somewhere far away. Out on the ocean a storm had risen and the boats carrying her father and brother were breaking apart — and in spirit she had gone to them, one hand gripping her father, her teeth clenched on her brother's clothing. Seeing her collapsed and unresponsive, her mother shook her awake in a panic. The instant her mouth opened to answer, the brother held in her teeth slipped away. Her father came home; her brother never did.

Lin Mo-niang was born in 960, the first year of the Jianlong era. Sharp from childhood, she could read scriptures by the age of eight, and she would stand at the shore reading the sky, guiding the village boats around the coming storms. In 987, at just twenty-eight, she passed away in serene meditation atop Meiyu Peak on Meizhou Island. The grateful villagers built her a shrine, and over the centuries one dynasty after another raised her titles — from 'Lady' to 'Heavenly Consort' and at last to 'Empress of Heaven, the Heavenly Holy Mother.' A fishing girl who could not save her own brother became the guardian of the entire Chinese seafaring world.
worship:
Offerings to Mazu are mainly vegetarian: fresh flowers, the 'four fruits,' longevity peaches, red tortoise cakes, and steamed fa-gao all suit her well. Mazu favors cleanliness, so keep the altar table tidy. How do you pray? On entering the temple, first offer incense at the Heaven Emperor censer, then step to Mazu's main altar and state your name, your address, and what you're asking for — safe voyages, career, marriage, or children are all fair to request.

The 23rd day of the third lunar month is Mazu's birthday, and for weeks around it processions wind across the whole island. If you want to feel it for yourself, walk a stretch alongside the Dajia or Baishatun pilgrimage and bow as the palanquin passes — for many Taiwanese, it is one of the most treasured moments of blessing all year.
festivals: Mazu's birthday on the 23rd of the 3rd lunar month is Taiwan's largest religious event. The 9-day pilgrimage from Dajia Jenn Lann Temple and the walking pilgrimage from Baishatun attract hundreds of thousands, ranking alongside Vatican Christmas Mass and the Hajj as one of the world's three great religious events.

temples.name: Dajia Zhenlan Temple
temples.deityStory: The Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage is Taiwan's largest religious event, a 9-day, 300km journey on foot, ranking among the world's top three religious events.

temples.name: Beigang Chaotian Temple
temples.deityStory: Beigang Chaotian Temple is a major center of Mazu worship, with branch temples worldwide. The road in front is a famous pilgrimage route.

temples.name: Baishatun Gongtian Temple
temples.deityStory: Famous for the 'Pink Supercar' palanquin. The pilgrimage route is unpredictable, guided solely by Mazu's will.

temples.name: Lugang Mazu Temple
temples.deityStory: Houses the 'Meizhou Mazu' statue gifted by Emperor Kangxi, the only temple in Taiwan with an original statue from the ancestral Meizhou temple.

temples.name: Taitung Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: The oldest Mazu temple in Eastern Taiwan, with over a century of history, serving as the religious center of Taitung.

temples.name: Songshan Ciyou Temple
temples.deityStory: Founded during the Qianlong era, it is the most important Mazu temple in Songshan and the spiritual center next to Raohe Night Market.

temples.name: Taichung Lecheng Temple
temples.deityStory: Known as 'Hanxi Mazu Temple', founded over 200 years ago during the Qianlong era. A major Mazu worship center in Taichung, also famous for its matchmaking deity.

temples.name: Changhua Nanyao Temple
temples.deityStory: The most important Mazu temple in Changhua, known for its unique 'Bengang pilgrimage' tradition and exquisite architecture.

temples.name: Shanbian Mazu Temple
temples.deityStory: A historic Mazu temple in Houlong, witnessing the early Han Chinese settlement history of Miaoli.

temples.name: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple
temples.deityStory: Originally the residence of the Ming Dynasty's Prince of Ningjing, converted to a Mazu temple during the Kangxi era. The first government-built Mazu temple in Taiwan.

temples.name: Xingang Fengtian Temple
temples.deityStory: One of Chiayi's most important Mazu temples, famous as the destination of the Dajia Mazu pilgrimage.

temples.name: Hualien Gang Tian Temple

temples.name: Penghu Tianhou Temple
temples.deityStory: The oldest Mazu temple in Taiwan, established during the Ming Dynasty and the most important religious center in Penghu.

name: Guan Sheng Di Jun (Lord Guan)
domain: God of war, wealth, loyalty and righteousness
description: Walk down any old street in Taiwan and look up at the little altars behind the shop counters — seven out of ten are watched over by the same red-faced, long-bearded figure. That's Guan Sheng Di Jun, better known to everyone as Guan Gong (Lord Guan) or Guan Yu. He began as a real man: a legendary general of the Three Kingdoms era whose Green Dragon Crescent Blade earned him a thousand years of fame. Yet in Taiwan he may be the hardest-working deity of all. Merchants worship him as a god of wealth; students pray to him for exam luck (Guan Yu was famous for never putting down his copy of the Spring and Autumn Annals); police officers and business owners come to him for integrity and justice. He is one of the rare historical figures venerated by three traditions at once — Confucians call him the 'Martial Sage,' Taoists crown him 'Guan Sheng Di Jun,' and Buddhists honor him as the Sangharama Bodhisattva. From Taipei's Xingtian Temple to Tainan's Martial Temple, his incense has burned unbroken for centuries — not because of his blade, but because of a single word he lived by: loyalty.
story:
Cao Cao may be the most heartbroken fan in Chinese history. After surrounding Guan Yu and accepting his surrender, the warlord showered him with everything a man could want — fine wine and feasts, a high title, and the legendary Red Hare, the finest horse in the land. Guan Yu accepted the horse (a warrior knows a good horse when he sees one) and nothing else. His mind was fixed on a single question: where was his sworn brother, Liu Bei?

The moment word arrived, Guan Yu took his two sisters-in-law under his protection and left. Cao Cao lined the road with five checkpoints to stop him; Guan Yu fought through every one — the feat remembered as 'crossing five passes and slaying six generals.' Riches, rank, and comfort were his for the taking, and he rode a thousand li away from all of it to rejoin a brother who at that moment had nothing.

That is the heart of it: he valued a promise more than his own life. And it is exactly why Taiwanese have trusted him for centuries. In business, the person you fear most is the one with no honor — so people hand their livelihoods to the god with the most.
worship:
What is Lord Guan best at answering? Prayers for honest prosperity and fair dealing in business, for passing exams, for justice, and for driving off evil all fall within his jurisdiction.

How to pray: set out your offerings, light incense, state your name and what you're asking for, then cast moon blocks to ask whether he grants it. What matters most is sincerity — Guan Gong has no patience for a false heart.

Offerings: the 'three meats' (a whole chicken, pork, and a whole fish), longevity peaches, longevity noodles, and three cups of clear tea. Some devotees lay a copy of the Spring and Autumn Annals on the altar as a mark of respect.

There is only one taboo, but it is the important one: come with clean intentions. If you're praying for ill-gotten money, save your incense — this is the god of righteous wealth, and he cannot abide a speck of grit in his eye.
festivals: The most important festival is Guan Sheng Di Jun's birthday on the 24th day of the 6th lunar month. Major celebrations are held at temples across Taiwan, including Xingtian Temple and Tainan's Martial Temple.

temples.name: Xingtian Temple
temples.deityStory: The busiest Guan Gong temple in northern Taiwan, and the first major temple to ban incense burning in 2014 — a bold environmental move. Just put your palms together and pray.

temples.name: Tainan Grand Martial Temple
temples.deityStory: The only Guan Gong temple historically included in official state ceremonies. Over 300 years old, and you can feel every year of it when you step inside.

temples.name: Jiaosi Xietian Temple
temples.deityStory: Perfect combo: soak in Jiaosi’s famous hot springs, then pay respects to Guan Gong.

name: Earth God (Tu Di Gong)
domain: Land protection, wealth and harvest, neighborhood safety
description: In Taiwan you can barely walk three steps without passing an Earth God shrine — they're packed in tighter than convenience stores. This white-bearded old grandfather carries the formal title Fude Zhengshen, but everyone just calls him Tudigong or Tudi Bo, a name that lands somewhere close to 'the kindly uncle at the end of the lane.' His portfolio is about as down-to-earth as divinity gets: safe homes, good harvests, neighborly peace, and — crucially — keeping the wallet from running too thin. Think of him as heaven's local ward chief. The shrines may be tiny, but no god is woven more deeply into daily Taiwanese life. Shopkeepers honor him with the 'zuoya' ritual on the 2nd and 16th of every lunar month, and the year's final zuoya, the 'weiya,' is the very reason Taiwanese companies throw their famous year-end employee banquets. From the little shrines at the edge of a rice field to the queues snaking around Nantou's Zinan Temple, the most unassuming god in Taiwan turns out to be the one people can least do without.
story: The most popular origin story runs like this. In the Zhou dynasty there was a tax official named Zhang Fude — and in an age when tax collectors were despised, he was so honest that he gave away his own salary to help the poor. He lived to 102, an almost unheard-of age back then. After he died, a farmer he had once helped built him a humble shrine out of three stones. And then something strange happened: the farmer's fortunes began to soar. Word got around, the neighbors built shrines of their own, and Earth God temples went up one after another — until they outnumbered every other kind of temple on the island. Call it the most successful word-of-mouth campaign in history. One honest official, starting from three stones after his death, became the most widespread god in all of Taiwan. No dazzling miracles, just the plainest of truths — that good people are repaid — which is exactly what makes Tudigong so endearing. He isn't remote and he isn't stern; he's the old neighbor who watched you grow up.
worship:
What to pray for: wealth (Tudigong is the most approachable of all the money gods), a safe home, a thriving business, a good harvest. Business owners, take note — you honor him with the 'zuoya' ritual on the 2nd and 16th of every lunar month. That's the old custom.

Praying to him is easy. The offerings needn't be grand — three meats, fruit, peanuts, mochi, candy, all of it works. Tudigong isn't a picky eater; sincerity is what counts. As you offer incense, tell him your address, your name, and what you're hoping for. To pray for wealth, burn 'Tudigong gold' paper money, or head to Zhushan Zinan Temple in Nantou to cast moon blocks and borrow 'prosperity money' as your seed capital.

There's just one taboo: if you borrow prosperity money, you must pay it back once your fortunes improve — usually double. Tudigong is a kind old soul, but his memory is excellent.
festivals: His birthday on the 2nd of the 2nd lunar month ('First Ya') sees celebrations at temples everywhere. The 'Last Ya' on the 16th of the 12th month evolved into Taiwan's unique corporate year-end banquet tradition, where traditionally a chicken pointing at an employee suggested they wouldn't be rehired.

temples.name: Zhushan Zinan Temple
temples.deityStory: Famous for lending 'prosperity money.' Devotees borrow small sums from the Earth God to start businesses, often returning double the amount after success.

temples.name: Checheng Fu'an Temple
temples.deityStory: The largest Earth God temple in Southeast Asia. Its furnace is famously called the 'God's Money Counter' — it automatically sucks in spirit money placed at the opening.

temples.name: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple
temples.deityStory: Northern Taiwan's most famous wealth temple, featuring a giant Earth God statue. Its mountain location offers stunning night views and it's open 24 hours.

associatedTemples: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple (Zhonghe District, New Taipei City)
Checheng Fu'an Temple (Checheng Township, Pingtung County)

name: Jade Emperor (Yu Huang Da Di)
domain: Ruler of Heaven, supreme deity, lord of all gods
description: In the dead of night on the ninth day of the first lunar month, many Taiwanese households stay awake on purpose. As the hour of zi strikes, an altar goes up in the open air and the whole family bows to the sky — three kneelings and nine kowtows. This is 'Tian Gong's birthday,' the feast day of the Jade Emperor, Yu Huang Da Di, whom Taiwanese affectionately call Tian Gong or Tian Gong Zu, the Heavenly Grandfather. He holds the highest rank in Taoism, ruling the three realms of heaven, earth, and water and presiding over every immortal and every living thing. Wind and rain, thunder and lightning, the turning of the seasons are his to arrange; the good and evil of humankind are his to review; and at year's end all the gods report back to his court. When a Taiwanese person is wronged, they look up and cry 'Oh, Grandfather Heaven!' — and the proverb says 'Heaven loves a good person.' Whether or not you ever set foot in his temple, Tian Gong already lives inside the Taiwanese language. To witness worship at its most exalted, go to the Jade Emperor's birthday at Tainan's Tiantan Temple: a whole night of blazing lamps and unbroken firecrackers.
story:
The Taoist scriptures say the Jade Emperor was once the crown prince of a realm called the Kingdom of Radiant Wonder and Bliss. Compassionate from boyhood, he governed his kingdom into perfect order after taking the throne — and then, at the very height of his glory, he gave the throne away and withdrew into the deep mountains to cultivate the Way. He cultivated for 1,750 kalpas, each one lasting 129,600 years, and only after an age longer still did he attain the rank of Jade Emperor and come to rule the three realms. Even the supreme Grandfather Heaven earned his place one step at a time; no one is simply born to that seat.

Folk tradition tells a homelier version. On the 25th day of the twelfth lunar month, the Jade Emperor comes down in person to inspect the deeds of humankind. People mind their words and actions especially on that day, because 'Heaven is watching.' In an age long before cameras, that single phrase was Taiwan's earliest system of self-restraint: even when no one can see you, someone up above is keeping the record.
worship:
Worshipping Tian Gong is the most exacting rite of all — no corners cut. The altar is set outdoors facing the open sky, in two tiers. The upper table is for the Jade Emperor himself: fresh flowers, candles, three cups of clear tea, five fruits, six vegetarian dishes, sweet rice cake, and red round cakes. The lower table is for his officials, laid with the five meats. Beside the altar stand two stalks of sugarcane bound with red thread, symbolizing a life that 'rises ever higher, joint by joint.' The spirit money must be the highest grade — 'Tian Gong gold.'

Timing matters too: on the ninth day of the first lunar month, worship begins at the hour of zi (11 p.m.) with the full three kneelings and nine kowtows, the most solemn ceremony of the entire year. The one taboo toward Tian Gong is a matter of attitude: offer only reverence. Better to keep the offerings and the ritual simple than to treat him with the slightest carelessness.
festivals: The Jade Emperor's birthday on the 9th of the 1st lunar month is one of Taiwan's most important religious holidays. Tainan Tiantan Temple hosts the grandest celebration, with firecrackers and lights through the night.

temples.name: Tainan Tiantan Temple
temples.deityStory: Known as the 'Temple of Heaven,' it's the first official Jade Emperor temple. Its famous 'One' plaque symbolizes that human calculations are no match for Heaven's will.

temples.name: Songshan Fengtian Temple
temples.deityStory: A grand Temple of Heaven in Taipei with thriving worship. Its magnificent architecture makes it a key site for prayers for peace and protection.

name: Yue Lao (Old Man Under the Moon)
domain: God of marriage, matchmaking, tying red threads of fate
description: In the days before Valentine's, the line outside Taipei's Xiahai City God Temple spills clear across the temple plaza — every one of them here to find Yue Lao. This deity, fondly called Yue Lao or Yue Lao Gong, the Old Man Under the Moon, runs a single line of business: matchmaking. In his hand he keeps the ledger of marriages, recording who is fated to whom; once he ties the red thread, two people will find each other no matter how far apart they start. Yue Lao's popularity in Taiwan is astonishing. On Qixi, on Western Valentine's Day, on any ordinary weekend, singles crowd the major Yue Lao temples to ask for a red thread — and Japanese tourists fly in especially to do the same. Just look at the thank-you wedding cakes at Xiahai: by the temple's own count, more than 6,000 couples come back each year to give thanks, which tells you plenty about the old man's success rate. However far technology advances, the most powerful dating algorithm in the Taiwanese heart is still that red thread in his hand.
story:
Yue Lao's classic entrance comes on a moonlit night in the Tang dynasty. A young scholar named Wei Gu came upon a white-bearded old man outside an inn, reading an enormous book by moonlight. Curious, Wei Gu asked what it was. 'This,' the old man said, 'is the ledger of every marriage in the world.'

Wei Gu pressed him at once: who was his own match? The old man flipped through the pages and pointed across the street to a grubby little girl in the arms of an old woman. 'Her.' Wei Gu was appalled — small, filthy, nothing like the bride he'd imagined — and in his fury he sent a man to kill her. The assassin lost his nerve and managed only to slash the child across the brow before fleeing.

Fourteen years later, Wei Gu married a beautiful young woman. On their wedding night he noticed a scar between her eyebrows, and when he asked about it, the truth came out: she was that very girl. He had run for fourteen years and traveled a full circle, only to end up at the other end of the red thread. A thousand years on, the story still makes one point: once Yue Lao ties the thread, not even a blade can cut it.
worship:
What to pray for: to find a partner, to be granted a good match, to smooth out a relationship. One caveat — Yue Lao deals only in 'true affinity.' If you're trying to break up a couple or steal someone else's partner, he won't take the case.

How to pray: first introduce yourself to Yue Lao (name, birthday, address, and your current relationship status), then sincerely describe the partner you're hoping for — be specific, but keep it reasonable. Ask for a red thread to carry home in your wallet; don't wash it and don't lose it, and keep it on you until you meet your match.

Recommended offerings: red dates, longan, peanuts, and lotus seeds — together they sound like 'may you soon have children' — plus a little candy to sweeten the romance.

The most important taboo: never bring an umbrella to Yue Lao. The word for 'umbrella' sounds exactly like the word for 'to part.' And once you've found your match, remember to bring your partner back with a box of wedding cakes to give thanks — nothing pleases Yue Lao more.
festivals: While there's no specific birthday festival, visitor numbers surge around Chinese Valentine's Day (7th of 7th lunar month) and February 14th. Xiahai Temple holds special matchmaking events during the Qixi Festival.

temples.name: Taipei Xiahai City God Temple
temples.deityStory: The Matchmaker God here is globally famous. Over 6,000 couples return annually with wedding cakes to give thanks — an amazing success rate.

temples.name: Taichung Lecheng Temple

temples.name: Tainan Grand Mazu Temple

temples.name: Tainan Grand Martial Temple
temples.deityStory: The Matchmaker God here is famous for 'cutting bad romances', helping worshippers end unhealthy relationships.

name: City God (Cheng Huang)
domain: City protection, underworld justice, rewarding good and punishing evil
description: Step into a City God temple and the first thing you see, hung above the doorway, is three characters: 'You have come.' If your conscience is clear it reads like a warm welcome; if it isn't, it sends a chill down your spine. This is Chenghuang Ye, the City God — also called Chenghuang Laoye or Chenghuang Zunshen — the local magistrate of the underworld. The world of the living has its county chiefs and mayors; the world below has its City God, and every wrong you got away with in life is tallied in his ledger. He is the underworld's judge, prosecutor, and chief of police rolled into one, and the giant abacus hanging in his hall is his calling card: good and evil are all counted in the end. Yet he is more than a figure of dread — he also guards the peace of his district, and he even comes ranked like the mortal civil service: a 'Metropolitan' City God governs a province, a 'Prefectural' one a prefecture, a 'County' one a county. Hsinchu's is the highest-ranking City God temple in all Taiwan. Thronged by day, heavy with atmosphere by night — that coexistence of the living and the dead is something only a City God temple can offer.
story:
Unlike most deities, the City God has no single fixed identity. Each locality's City God is usually a fair-minded, well-respected figure from that place, appointed to the post after death — which means Taipei's City God and Tainan's City God are, quite literally, different men. There's something moving in that idea: live an upright life, and one day it may be your turn to watch over a stretch of land.

What the temples share is their furnishings. Over the door hangs the plaque 'You have come,' like a greeting that has been waiting a long time. Inside the hall hangs the great abacus, a reminder that every account is on the books. And flanking the shrine stand two figures — one tall, one short, one black-faced, one white — General Xie and General Fan, the Black and White Impermanence, who bring in those whose time has come. Plenty of Taiwanese remember being led into a City God temple as a child and not daring to look up at those looming statues. Only later do you understand: what frightened you was never the statue. It was the ledger in your own heart.
worship:
What do people pray for here? Justice and a fair hearing (many come before a lawsuit), relief from backstabbers and petty enemies, and safety for the neighborhood. Quite a few City God temples also house a startlingly effective Yue Lao — Taipei's Xiahai City God Temple alone receives thousands of boxes of thank-you wedding cakes every year.

How to pray: bring the three meats and wine, offer incense first at the Heaven Emperor censer, then step to the City God's main hall and state your name, address, and request. If you're seeking redress for a wrong, you can write out your grievance and burn it as a petition. Keep the offerings on the formal side — three meats, wine, and spirit money, nothing too offhand.

The great taboo: never lie or swear a false oath inside a City God temple. He is the one who keeps the accounts, and lying to his face is walking straight into the net.
festivals: The City God's birthday on the 13th of the 5th lunar month is the most important festival. Taipei Xiahai's procession has over a century of history, while Hsinchu's combines elaborate parades with its century-old night market food culture.

temples.name: Taipei Xiahai City God Temple
temples.deityStory: Locally famous for its Matchmaker God (Yue Lao). Thousands of couples return with wedding cakes to give thanks, making it Taiwan's top spot for finding love.

temples.name: Hualien City God Temple
temples.deityStory: One of the oldest temples in Hualien, protecting the people of the east coast.

temples.name: Hsinchu City God Temple
temples.deityStory: The highest-ranking City God Temple in Taiwan. Its procession, combined with the century-old night market, creates a unique 'faith + food' culture.

temples.name: Chiayi City God Temple
temples.deityStory: The most important City God Temple in Chiayi with centuries of history. The annual City God procession is a major religious event.

temples.name: Kinmen Wudao City God Temple
temples.deityStory: The most important City God Temple in Kinmen, dating back to the Ming Dynasty and serving as the spiritual center for locals.

name: God of Wealth (Cai Shen)
domain: Lord of wealth, attracting fortune, business prosperity
description: In the small hours of the fifth day of the first lunar month, shops all over Taiwan wake almost as one. Firecrackers go off up and down the street as every business flings open its doors to 'welcome the God of Wealth.' The guest of honor is Cai Shen Ye, and the form most Taiwanese greet is the martial god of wealth Zhao Gongming, also known as Xuantan Zhenjun. Add his four generals of the east, west, south, and north, and together they make the 'Five-Route God of Wealth,' symbolizing money rolling in from every direction. His job description is the bluntest of any deity's: he handles cash. Merchants pray for booming business, office workers for a raise, lottery players for a windfall — and Taiwanese pray in a wonderfully practical way, bringing their bankbooks, business cards, and receipts to the temple to be passed through the incense smoke, or queuing at Zhushan Zinan Temple in Nantou to borrow 'prosperity money' as seed capital, a custom that draws millions of visits a year. To soak up the wealth energy, head to Beigang Wude Temple in Yunlin, the founding ancestral temple of the Five-Route God of Wealth, where the 'Heavenly Treasury' furnace — said to be the largest in the world — is a sight in itself.
story:
Zhao Gongming's story is set down in The Investiture of the Gods — and, tellingly, he began on the losing side. In the last days of the Shang dynasty, Zhao Gongming had cultivated for years on Mount Emei and commanded formidable Taoist arts. When the Zhou rose in rebellion, he was called down to defend the Shang; riding a black tiger and wielding an iron whip, he left Jiang Ziya's army helpless. In the end Jiang Ziya resorted to a secret curse, the 'Nail-Head Seven-Arrow Book,' and drained Zhao Gongming of his life force — a master brought down not on the battlefield but by treachery.

When the time came to enthrone the gods, Jiang Ziya weighed the whole of Zhao's life: he had backed the wrong side, yes, but he was loyal, righteous, and deeply accomplished. So he was crowned Zhenjun of the Mysterious Altar and given command of four generals — attracting wealth, bringing treasure, gathering gems, and turning profit. He lost the war and won a thousand years of incense. The most important god of wealth in the Chinese world is a loyal, honorable man who lost and yet came out ahead — a reminder to everyone who prays here that what the God of Wealth respects is money earned the right way.
worship:
Offerings here lean into wealth and good omens: fa-gao 'prosperity cake,' pineapple (which sounds like 'fortune arriving'), oranges (for great luck), apples (for peace), and gold-ingot-shaped pastries are especially fitting, with 'God of Wealth gold' for the spirit money. Business owners often set out five fruits beside the cash register.

The most distinctly Taiwanese approach is to bring your bankbook, business cards, or receipts to the temple and pass them through the incense smoke for a blessing. You can also cast moon blocks at Zhushan Zinan Temple to borrow NT$600 in prosperity money as seed capital — just remember to pay it back with interest the following year.

Key dates: the 'welcoming the God of Wealth' opening on the fifth day of the first lunar month, and the zuoya rituals on the 2nd and 16th of each month. Pray for honest earnings and a thriving career — and if it's crooked money you're after, don't bother asking.
festivals: The 5th of the 1st lunar month ('Welcoming Wealth God') is the key festival. Businesses fire crackers at midnight and burn spirit money. Opening for business on this day is called 'Breaking the Five,' symbolizing a prosperous start to the year.

temples.name: Beigang Wude Temple
temples.deityStory: The ancestral temple of the Five Paths God of Wealth in Taiwan. Its massive 'Heavenly Treasury' furnace is claimed to be the world's largest, symbolizing abundant wealth.

temples.name: Zhushan Zinan Temple
temples.deityStory: Though dedicated to the Earth God, it's revered as a wealth temple due to its efficacy. The tradition of borrowing prosperity money draws crowds year-round.

temples.name: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple
temples.deityStory: Devotees come to exchange 'mother money' — swapping large bills for coins to keep in wallets as wealth charms. The giant Earth God statue is a northern Taiwan landmark.

associatedTemples: Beigang Wude Temple (Beigang Township, Yunlin County)

name: Wenchang Dijun (God of Culture and Literature)
description: When exam season comes around, the offering tables at a Wenchang temple pile up with a little mountain of photocopied admission tickets, flanked by scallions, celery, and radishes — the standard scene of Taiwanese students praying to Wenchang Dijun. Wenchang Dijun, also called Wenchang Gong or Zitong Dijun, is the deity in charge of examinations and scholarly fame: in imperial times he decided who placed first in the civil exams, and today he oversees the college entrance test, the national civil service exams, and professional certifications — anything with a score attached is his department. For Taiwanese, praying to Wenchang before a test is as routine as a Japanese student's visit to a Tenmangu shrine. And it's often not just the candidate who shows up — grandmother, mother, and the aunties from down the street all come to help, a whole family clustered before a single altar. If Taiwanese family solidarity has a home address, it's the Wenchang temple at exam time. Taipei's Wenchang Temple near Shuanglian is papered wall to wall with admission-ticket copies every testing season; if you're passing by, step in and feel the whole-nation cram-mode in the air.
story:
Wenchang Dijun is the celestial star-lord who governs 'literary fortune' — everything to do with learning and examinations falls under his charge. Folklore tells a story with real flavor. A scholar had failed the exams so many times that he was ready to give up. One night he dreamed of Wenchang Dijun, who told him: 'You're not short on intelligence — you're short on effort. Go back and read the material one more time.' The scholar woke, threw himself into study, and in the end topped the list.

The point isn't 'pray and you'll pass.' It's that Wenchang helps those who are already putting in the work. He's no wish-granting machine; he's more like a strict but fair teacher. Read what you're supposed to read, and he'll look after your luck on the day — but if you spent the run-up gaming instead of studying, no amount of incense will save you, because Wenchang can see. Of all the gods, he's the one most like a teacher.
worship:
What to pray for: the college entrance test, national civil service exams, graduate admissions, professional certifications — plus academic improvement, promotion reviews, and finishing a thesis.

How to pray: bring a photocopy of your admission ticket, offer incense, and state your name, the type of exam, its date, and its location; then pass the copy through the incense smoke, take it home, and tuck it inside your textbook.

The offerings are one long string of puns: scallion (which sounds like 'clever'), celery ('diligent'), radish ('good fortune'), a rice dumpling ('sure to pass'), and osmanthus cake (evoking the classical image of 'plucking osmanthus in the moon palace' for exam success). The humor of Taiwanese temple offerings hits its peak at Wenchang's altar.

The one crucial taboo: never bring duck eggs. Scoring zero on a test is called 'getting a duck egg' — so bringing duck eggs to Wenchang is essentially praying to fail.
festivals: His birthday is the 3rd of the 2nd lunar month. During exam seasons, temples hold grand blessing ceremonies where priests light lamps and perform rituals to 'open wisdom' for nervous students.

temples.name: Taipei Wenchang Temple
temples.deityStory: Located near Shuanglian MRT, this is Taipei's most popular Wenchang temple. During exam season, the interior is literally wallpapered with exam permit copies.

temples.name: Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia)
temples.deityStory: Wenchang Pavilion in the Chihkan Tower complex enshrines Wenchang Dijun and Kui Xing, a key place for Tainan students to pray for exam success.

associatedTemples: Chihkan Tower (Haishen Temple/Wenchang Pavilion) (West Central District, Tainan City)

name: Baosheng Dadi (Great Emperor of Life Protection)
domain: God of medicine, healing, health protection
description: Look closely at a statue of Baosheng Dadi and you'll often find a tiger crouched at his side — not a decoration, but a patient. Legend says this god of medicine, known as Dadao Gong or Wu Zhenren (the True Man Wu), once reached bare-handed into a tiger's throat to pull out a lodged bone; the grateful beast never left him again. Baosheng Dadi was born Wu Tao, a celebrated physician of Tong'an in Fujian during the Northern Song. His skill was extraordinary and he treated rich and poor without distinction, and after his death the Hokkien people enshrined him as their foremost god of medicine. Settlers carried his faith across to Taiwan, where the incense for health and healing has never gone out — even doctors, nurses, and pharmacists honor him as the patron of their profession, and some temples still offer traditional 'medicine lots,' herbal prescriptions drawn by divination. His flagship temple, Taipei's Dalongdong Baoan Temple, won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award for its restoration; if you want to see Taiwanese temple craftsmanship at its peak, this is where you go.
story:
Wu Tao's most famous house call was to the reigning Empress Dowager herself. When the mother of Emperor Renzong of Song lay ill and no remedy worked, Wu Tao cured her. The emperor offered to make him Imperial Physician — wealth and status in a single step — but he turned it down, asking only to go home and keep treating ordinary people, buying medicine out of his own pocket for those who couldn't pay.

He was born in 979 in Baijiao village, Tong'an, Fujian, and mastered internal and external medicine, acupuncture, and herbal lore, with a special gift for fighting epidemics. In 1036, at the age of fifty-eight, he fell from a cliff while gathering herbs on a mountainside — a healer who died on the very path of his healing. The villagers built a temple in his memory and honored him as Baosheng Dadi, the Great Emperor Who Protects Life.

Taiwanese folklore adds a fond footnote: Dadao Gong and Mazu were once a couple who later parted. Every third lunar month, they say, he sends wind to tangle her hair and she sends rain to soak him through — which is why the weather that month swings so wildly between gusts and showers, a pattern locals nickname 'Dadao Gong's wind, Mazu's rain.'
worship:
Worship Baosheng Dadi with cleanliness in mind — the offerings are simple: fresh flowers, vegetarian fruit, and clear tea, with sincerity counting for the most. What is he best asked for? Recovery from illness, health and safety, and the warding off of misfortune — even doctors, nurses, and pharmacists come to pay respects to the patron of their trade.

Some temples keep 'medicine lots': after casting moon blocks you draw a slip and take the prescription to a Chinese herbal pharmacy. Modern temples are careful to add a reminder, though — the lots are for the comfort of the heart, and anyone who feels unwell should still see a doctor.

The 15th day of the third lunar month is his birthday, when Baoan Temple's months-long 'Baosheng Cultural Festival' fills the calendar with clan operas, fire-walking rites, and arts events — carrying the old spirit of 'healing the world' right into the present day.
festivals: His birthday on the 15th of the 3rd lunar month kicks off the three-month 'Baosheng Cultural Festival' at Baoan Temple, one of Taiwan's largest temple cultural events, featuring traditional opera, fire-walking rituals, and art exhibitions.

temples.name: Dalongdong Baoan Temple
temples.deityStory: Winner of the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award for its exquisite architecture. The annual Baosheng Cultural Festival is a major event in Taipei.

associatedTemples: Dalongdong Baoan Temple (Datong District, Taipei City)

name: Xuantian Shangdi (Supreme Emperor of Dark Heaven)
domain: Exorcism, nation protection, guardian of the north
description: One foot on a turtle, one on a snake, hair loose and feet bare, a Seven-Star Sword in his hand — the silhouette is unmistakable. This is Xuantian Shangdi, the Supreme Emperor of the Dark Heaven, known to most Taiwanese as Shangdi Gong or Diye Gong and also called Zhenwu Dadi or the Emperor of the North Pole. His rank in Taoism is exalted: he governs the seven stars of the north and commands the celestial position of the Dark Warrior. In Taiwan he is famed above all for his ferocity against demons — when something feels haunted, jinxed, or unclean, Shangdi Gong is the name many people reach for first, and countless spirit mediums and Taoist priests serve him as their patron. Every third day of the third lunar month, his birthday draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims to Songboling Shoutian Temple in Nantou, the head temple from which more Xuantian Shangdi shrines branch than from anywhere else in Taiwan. One more detail worth noticing: he belongs to the North, whose element is Water and whose color is black — which is why his statues and his temples tend to be draped in dark tones.
story:
The most widely told legend is a butcher's story. In a past life, Xuantian Shangdi was a butcher weighed down by the karma of endless killing. One day an immortal opened his eyes to the truth, and in a fit of remorse he resolved to lay down his knife and atone — he cut open his own belly and drew out his stomach and intestines as a sign of repentance. But the intestines fell into the water and became a snake, and the stomach became a turtle, and the two of them stirred up the waters and terrorized the people.

Through long cultivation the butcher's soul at last attained godhood. Yet the turtle and the snake were his own karma, and no one else could clean up after him — so he pins them beneath his own feet, holding them down for all time. That is why his statue forever stands upon a turtle and a snake: they are not mounts, but the past he conquered. Lay down the butcher's knife, and even the gravest sin has a chance at a fresh start — but the karma you create is yours alone to face. That is the sharpest lesson this fierce warrior-god leaves for us. (The more orthodox Taoist account tells it differently: he was an incarnation of Laozi who cultivated for forty-two years on Mount Wudang before ascending to godhood.)
worship: Offerings to Xuantian Shangdi include the three meats, five fruits, tea, and wine. Because of the butcher legend in his past, some temples avoid pork and use chicken, fish, or vegetarian dishes instead — it's safest to ask the temple first. What is he best asked for? Driving off evil, 'soul-calming' (shoujing), and breaking curses are his specialty: parents bring frightened children for a soul-calming rite, homeowners pray to settle a house before moving in or breaking ground, and anyone who feels they've brushed against something unclean can ask the temple for 'purifying talisman water' to sprinkle and clear it away. Around his birthday on the third day of the third lunar month, temples hold fire-walking rites and the 'passing beneath the palanquin' ritual, and the surge of pilgrims to Songboling Shoutian Temple is the event of the year.
festivals: His birthday on the 3rd of the 3rd lunar month sees massive celebrations, especially at Songboling Shoutian Temple, attracting hundreds of thousands. Traditional rituals include fire-walking and passing under sedan chairs.

temples.name: Songboling Shoutian Temple
temples.deityStory: The head temple with the most Xuantian Shangdi branches in Taiwan. Located on the Bagua Mountain range, it offers great views and is a major pilgrimage center.

associatedTemples: Songboling Shoutian Temple (Mingjian Township, Nantou County)

name: Confucius
description: Walk into a Confucius temple and you'll notice three strange things: there's no god statue, no burning of spirit money, and no medium telling fortunes. The one enshrined here is Confucius, honored as the Supreme Sage and First Teacher and the Model Teacher for Ten Thousand Ages — an educator of China's Spring and Autumn period. Named Kong Qiu, styled Zhongni, he founded the Confucian school, and after more than two thousand years of veneration he is revered as the guardian of scholars and teachers. Almost every county and city in Taiwan has a Confucius temple, and with spirit tablets in place of statues and formal bows in place of worship, it is the most restrained and most ceremonious form of temple on the island. Around Teachers' Day on September 28 each year, Confucius temples hold the 'Shidian' ceremony, in which the chief celebrant follows the ancient rites and rows of dancers present music and dance passed down for a thousand years — the most fully preserved traditional ceremonial music in Taiwan. To see where it all began, visit the Tainan Confucius Temple: founded in 1665 under the Ming-loyalist Zheng regime, it was the first official Confucius temple in Taiwan, and the words 'The First Academy of Taiwan' still hang above its gate.
story:
By worldly measures, Confucius's life was not a success. He was born in the state of Lu at the close of the Spring and Autumn period; he lost his father young, grew up poor, and found his footing through relentless study. In middle age he spent fourteen years traveling from state to state, promoting a political vision built on benevolence, righteousness, and propriety — and met closed doors everywhere he went, for not a single ruler truly put him to use.

In his later years he returned to Lu and did the one thing that would echo for two thousand years: he taught. He took in three thousand disciples, seventy-two of them sages, and edited the Six Classics. Confucius died in 479 BC at the age of seventy-three. The teacher who went unappreciated in life was raised up by one dynasty after another after his death, from 'King of Culture' to 'Great Sage and First Teacher of Great Completion.'

In 1665, Zheng Jing built Taiwan's first official Confucius temple in Tainan; and during the Japanese colonial era, under the pressure of a foreign culture, Taiwanese gentry insisted on keeping the rites to Confucius alive. A man who met walls everywhere in life became teacher to an entire civilization — his story is itself the finest proof that education can change the world.
worship:
Worshipping Confucius is nothing like worshipping the other gods: no offerings, no incense, no spirit money. You simply bow three times before his spirit tablet in the temple hall. This is the Confucian spirit of 'reverence without petition' — you honor the teacher rather than beg him for miracles. Students and parents often come before major exams to pray for academic success, and reciting a passage from the Analects suits the occasion well.

For spectacle, time your visit to the grand Confucius ceremony: around Teachers' Day on September 28, temples perform the Shidian rite, complete with the welcoming of the spirit, the three offerings, and the stately rows of ceremonial dancers. The 'wisdom cake' handed out afterward symbolizes a share of Confucius's wisdom and is the most coveted keepsake of all — for a student facing exams, a single piece is more reassuring than any protective charm.
associatedTemples: Tainan Confucius Temple (West Central District, Tainan City)

name: Ji Gong (Mad Monk)
domain: Saving the world, subduing demons, helping the weak and poor
description: Broken hat, broken fan, broken shoes, a tattered monk's robe, and a gourd of wine swinging from one hand — the least god-like god of all is Ji Gong, also known as the Living Buddha Ji Gong or the Mad Monk Ji. He began as a real Southern Song monk, the Chan master Daoji, who drank wine, ate meat, and behaved like a lunatic, yet cured the illnesses no one else could and threw himself into fighting for the wronged. The line he left behind — 'Wine and meat pass through the gut; the Buddha stays in the heart' — is still quoted today. In Taiwan, Ji Gong is the most down-to-earth deity there is: he pays no mind to status, prizes loyalty above all, and is beloved especially by laborers and small business owners. When Ji Gong 'descends' at a temple festival, the spirit medium drinks, waves the fan, and hops about — the liveliest act on the whole grounds. That ragged look isn't poverty; it's his signboard, a way of smashing every hollow formality to point straight at the true nature of the heart. Having bowed before so many solemn, upright gods, a lot of people find they can finally relax in front of Ji Gong.
story:
Ji Gong was born Li Xiuyuan in 1148, into a scholarly family in Tiantai, Zhejiang. As a young man he took vows at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou and received the dharma name Daoji — and then proceeded to scandalize the entire monastery, drinking, eating meat, and talking like a madman until the exasperated monks nicknamed him 'Ji the Lunatic.' Yet the mad monk had genuine power: he would tear scraps from his ragged robe, roll them into pills, and cure stubborn diseases with them, and he made a habit of helping the poor and punishing the cruel.

His most famous legend is 'the Flying Peak.' Ji Gong foresaw that a mountain peak was about to come hurtling down onto a village. He ran through the streets shouting a warning, but no one believed him — so in desperation he snatched a bride right out of the middle of her own wedding and bolted. The whole village gave chase to get her back, and as they poured out after him, the peak crashed down and flattened the now-empty village. Only then did they understand: the madman had saved every one of them.

In 1204, Daoji passed away at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou, leaving behind a verse: 'Sixty years of tumbling wall to wall; now gathered home, the water still meets the boundless blue.' A mad life, and a clear-eyed one.
worship:
Praying to Ji Gong is probably the most relaxed act of worship in all of Taiwan — because the offerings can include wine and meat. Rice wine, drunken chicken, braised snacks, fruit: all fair game. It's the exact opposite of the vegetarian rule most gods keep, and that's entirely in character for the god of no formality.

What to pray for? Saving people is his trade: healing illness and averting disaster, breaking a run of bad luck, standing up for the underdog, seeking justice. Some temples keep the tradition of Ji Gong 'descending' to handle cases, with the medium drinking and waving his fan in a re-creation of the mad monk's style.

The taboos here are the fewest of all: no elaborate ritual is required, and a sincere heart is what works. But don't misread 'wine and meat pass through the gut.' He may not stand on ceremony, but the one thing he weighs most is whether your heart is true.
festivals: His birthday falls on the 2nd of the 2nd lunar month (some temples celebrate on the 3rd of the 10th month). Temple festivals feature spirit medium sessions where mediums channel Ji Gong's eccentric behavior — a highly entertaining spectacle.

temples.name: Yilan Sanqing Temple
temples.deityStory: Set in a serene landscape. As a major Taoist temple, it also enshrines Ji Gong and is a must-visit for spiritual cultivators.

name: Queen Mother of the West (Xi Wangmu)
aliases: Golden Mother of the Jade Pond
domain: Immortality, ruler of the Jade Pond paradise, chief of all female immortals
description: Taiwanese celebrate birthdays with 'longevity peaches' — and the custom traces straight back to the immortality peaches of Wangmu Niangniang, the Queen Mother of the West. Wangmu Niangniang, also known as Xi Wangmu, the Golden Mother of the Jade Pond, or Jinmu Niangniang, is the most exalted goddess in Taoism, honored as 'chief of all immortals and most revered of the female immortals.' In myth she dwells at the Jade Pond on Mount Kunlun and tends the flat peaches that ripen just once every three thousand years and confer eternal life. Her care falls especially on women — she grants blessings and long life, oversees marriage and family harmony, and guides the cultivation of female immortals, which is why women hold her in particular reverence. In Taiwan, her worship centers on Hualien: the Cihui Tang movement that grew up from 1949 onward enshrines the Golden Mother of the Jade Pond as its principal deity and pairs the old spirit-writing tradition with medical care, elderly support, and other charitable work, making it one of the most vital systems in contemporary Taiwanese folk belief. Next time you bite into a longevity peach, remember the ancient goddess standing behind that taste of sweetness, keeping watch over her peach garden.
story:
Xi Wangmu may have undergone the most dramatic makeover of any deity. In her earliest appearance in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, she is a half-divine, half-bestial figure — human face, tiger's teeth, leopard's tail, wild unbound hair — dwelling on Mount Kunlun and presiding over heavenly disasters and punishments, nothing at all like the gentle Queen Mother of later ages. By the Han dynasty, in texts such as the Biography of King Mu of Zhou, she had transformed into a beautiful goddess who holds the elixir of immortality, meets King Mu at the Jade Pond, and gifts immortal peaches to Emperor Wu of Han.

Once Taoism took shape in the Wei and Jin periods, Xi Wangmu was honored as the chief of all female immortals, with the Jade Pond as her home and the flat peach as her emblem — three thousand years to blossom, three thousand to fruit, three thousand to ripen. Her 'Peach Banquet' is the grandest feast in heaven, and the very occasion Sun Wukong throws into chaos in Journey to the West. From beast-god to mother-goddess, this reversal across a thousand years mirrors how people's image of 'the mother' itself evolved. And in Taiwan, from 1949 onward, Hualien's Cihui Tang took her worship in yet another direction — compassion for the world and service to society — bringing the goddess down from the Jade Pond and into human life.
worship:
Offerings to the Queen Mother follow the vegetarian principle: fresh flowers, fruit, clear tea, and cakes, with a few peaches set out for good measure — a fitting echo of the immortality peach and its symbolism of long life. Common recitations include the Sutra of the Queen Mother's Sacred Virtue and the Heart Mantra of the Golden Mother of the Jade Pond.

What to pray for? Longevity and health, family harmony, marital accord, and filial children — she is held in special reverence by older women devotees. Women drawn to cultivation and sutra recitation can also enter the Cihui Tang system, which has always prized women's participation.

The 18th day of the seventh lunar month is her birthday, popularly called the Peach Banquet, when Hualien hosts the largest celebrations, with chanting, spirit-writing, and almsgiving. For an ordinary visit, come with a clean and quiet heart — the Golden Mother prizes purity, just like her Jade Pond.
festivals: The Queen Mother's birthday on the 18th of the 7th lunar month, known as the 'Peach Banquet,' is the most important festival. Cihui halls and Taoist temples across Taiwan hold grand celebrations with sutra chanting, spirit-writing, almsgiving, and cultural performances.

temples.name: Hualien Shen An Temple
temples.deityStory: Hualien's most famous Queen Mother temple and an important center of the Cihui Hall system. Legend says the Queen Mother appeared here to guide the temple's construction.

associatedTemples: Hualien Shen An Temple (Hualien City, Hualien County)

name: Lü Dongbin (Patriarch Lü)
description: On Zhinan Mountain above Muzha in Taipei sits Zhinan Temple, and its principal deity is Lü Dongbin, first of the Eight Immortals, revered by the faithful as Patriarch Lü, Lü Xiangong, or Fuyou Dijun. This immortal was accomplished in both the pen and the sword: a master swordsman whose 'flying sword that slays demons' tales spread far and wide, and a scholar by background, so that students pray to him for exam luck while Taoist cultivators honor him as the patriarch of internal alchemy. What Taiwanese know him best for, though, may be the legend that couples should never visit Zhinan Temple together — supposedly Patriarch Lü grows jealous and splits them up. The temple has clarified this many times: it's pure folk gossip, and in fact Lü only severs 'bad-luck romances' while safeguarding true love. Gossip aside, Zhinan Temple has long been called 'the foremost sacred mountain under heaven,' and its 'Immortal Patriarch oracle' is among the most famous divination slips in Taiwan. The insider's way to visit is to climb up at dusk, pay respects to the patriarch, and take in the glittering Taipei skyline on the way down.
story:
Before he was an immortal, Lü Dongbin was a scholar who kept failing his exams. In the Tang dynasty he traveled to Chang'an again and again to sit the imperial examination, and again and again his name was left off the list. The night that changed everything happened in a Chang'an tavern, where he met the immortal Zhongli Quan cooking a pot of millet. While the pot simmered, Lü dozed off — and in his dream he passed the exam, rose through office step by step, took a wife, raised children, and reached the highest ranks, only to be framed by scheming rivals and end up ruined, his family scattered, wandering the streets.

He woke with a start. The millet still wasn't done.

An entire lifetime of glory and ruin, gone in less time than it takes to cook one pot of grain — this is the origin of the idiom 'a golden millet dream.' On the spot, Lü Dongbin saw through the hunger for fame, took Zhongli Quan as his master, and went on to pass the 'Ten Trials' of desire, wealth, and mortal fear before attaining immortality. Rather than retreat into the mountains, he wandered the human world saving people; the carefree tale of 'thrice drunk at Yueyang Tower' still survives. Of all the Eight Immortals, this failed exam candidate is the most warmly human.
worship:
Worship Patriarch Lü with an emphasis on purity: clear tea, fruit, and vegetarian dishes. Because Lü was a scholar by background, exam-takers often add a writing brush, ink, paper, and an inkstone to the offering, a nod to his blessing over learning. What to pray for? Exam success, progress in cultivation, and the warding off of misfortune all fall within his scope.

At Zhinan Temple, don't leave without drawing an 'Immortal Patriarch oracle' — one of the most renowned divination slips in Taiwan, and the whole reason many people make the climb.

The 14th day of the fourth lunar month is Patriarch Lü's birthday, when Zhinan Temple pairs the birthday rites with poetry readings and calligraphy exhibitions, fitting for this most scholarly of immortals. And should couples steer clear? The temple's own answer: Lü only cuts off the bad romances — true love has nothing to fear.
festivals: His birthday on the 14th of the 4th lunar month features grand celebrations at Zhinan Temple, combining Taoist rituals with literary events like poetry readings and calligraphy exhibitions — fitting his scholarly immortal character.

temples.name: Zhinan Temple
temples.deityStory: Famous temple of Patriarch Lü in the north. Folk legend warns couples against visiting, but the temple clarifies that Lü only cuts bad relationships, while protecting true love.

associatedTemples: Zhinan Temple (Wenshan District, Taipei City)

name: Tai Sui (Grand Duke Jupiter)
domain: Annual fortune, averting misfortune, neutralizing yearly afflictions
description: Every year in the run-up to Lunar New Year, the news runs the same fixed story: 'These zodiac signs offend Tai Sui this year!' And then the lines form in front of the Tai Sui halls at temples across Taiwan — this is the island's annual appointment with Tai Sui Xingjun, popularly known as Tai Sui Ye or the Presiding Year God. Tai Sui is the deity who governs each year's fortune, and there are sixty of them rotating in step with the sexagenary calendar cycle. When your zodiac animal clashes with or is 'punished' by the current year's Tai Sui, you have 'offended Tai Sui' — believed to make for a bumpy, misfortune-prone year. So 'settling Tai Sui' became the most common annual ritual in Taiwan: at the start of the year you light a Tai Sui lamp at the temple, and at year's end you return to thank him. The saying 'don't break ground on Tai Sui's head' has long since left religion behind to become everyday speech, a warning against provoking a power beyond your weight. Four or five signs take their turn every year, so Tai Sui Ye never runs short of visitors.
story:
The root of the Tai Sui belief is, of all things, astronomy. The ancients observed that Jupiter — the 'Year Star' — circles the celestial sphere roughly every twelve years, so they divided the sky into twelve zones; each year Jupiter passed through one, and that zone had its own Tai Sui spirit on watch. Over time this grew into the full system of sixty Tai Sui in rotation, each with his own name and rank.

Folklore adds a story to make your skin crawl. Long ago, someone who scoffed at the taboo deliberately dug into the ground in the Tai Sui's direction — and unearthed a lump of flesh that kept growing and could not be cut through no matter what. Terrified, he hastily reburied it and set up an altar to it, and from then on the warning spread: never break ground on Tai Sui's head.

The curious part is that the 'Tai Sui fungus' in the tale really does exist — an underground fungus shaped like a mass of flesh, exactly the kind of thing that would unnerve the ancients. One belief, with one end tied to the stars and the other to a mystery buried in the soil: Tai Sui may be the most cross-disciplinary god of them all.
worship:
How do you 'settle Tai Sui'? Early in the lunar year — ideally before the 15th of the first month — you register your name and birth date at a temple, and the staff install a Tai Sui lamp or talisman in the Tai Sui hall, asking Tai Sui Xingjun to watch over you for the year. At year's end, around the twelfth lunar month, you return to 'thank Tai Sui,' closing the loop.

Who needs to do it? The signs that hold, clash with, punish, break, or harm the current year's Tai Sui — the temples and the media publish the list every year.

Advice for an offending year: wear a Tai Sui talisman, light a Tai Sui lamp, put off big changes like moving house or switching jobs, and do plenty of good deeds. When it comes to fortune, a little caution never hurt anyone.
festivals: The peak period for placing Tai Sui is from the 8th to 9th of the 1st lunar month. Major temples see long queues. The annual announcement of which zodiac signs 'offend' Tai Sui is a regular media event before each Lunar New Year.

temples.name: Songshan Ciyou Temple
temples.deityStory: Though primarily a Mazu temple, its Tai Sui Hall is grand and popular. The Tai Sui lamps here are renowned for their efficacy.
